hook.text: Smokers know smoking causes cancer. But each one believes they'll be the exception. That's optimism bias.

buildup.text: Optimism bias makes people believe bad things are less likely to happen to them than to others.

discovery.text: Tali Sharot found that the brain updates beliefs more for good news than bad. Asymmetric updating.

twist.text: It's actually useful: optimists try harder, persist longer, and recover faster from setbacks.

climax.text: But it kills planning. Projects run over budget and schedule because we underestimate what can go wrong.

punchline.text: Hope for the best. Plan for the worst.

quiz.question: How does optimism bias affect planning?
options: It leads to underestimating risks and timelines

details.summary: Most people believe they are less likely than average to experience negative events and more likely to experience positive ones. This optimism bias persists despite contradicting evidence and affects planning, risk assessment, and health behavior across cultures.
details.whyItMatters: Optimism bias drives under-preparation for risks and over-prediction of success. It partly explains why projects exceed budgets, why people under-insure, and why smokers believe they will avoid cancer.
takeaways: People underestimate personal risk relative to others
The bias persists across cultures and demographics
It contributes to the planning fallacy and risky behavior

faq.question: Does optimism bias have any benefits?
faq.answer: Moderate optimism supports mental health, motivation, and resilience. People with optimism bias experience less anxiety and take more initiative. However, excessive optimism leads to inadequate preparation and dangerous risk-taking. The right balance maximizes both wellbeing and realism.

faq.question: How does optimism bias affect project planning?
faq.answer: People consistently underestimate how long tasks will take and how much they will cost, known as the planning fallacy. They focus on the ideal scenario rather than base rates of similar past projects. Reference class forecasting, using outcomes from comparable projects, is the best antidote.
